items.text: ​Dancing About Architecture: Liminal Shot in an unfinished brutalist building in Accra, the short movement film Liminal captures a space caught between use and abandonment, and what remains when an undertaking goes unresolved. Directed by visual artist Naafia Naahemaa and produced by Dominique Petit-Frère, performer Nana Yaa Poku Asare-Boadu inhabits the structure through responsive, unchoreographed movement, navigating raw concrete staircases and exposed pillars to an original score by Malick Koly. - Naafia Naahemaa Observing the Ghanaian capital as a landscape shaped by perpetual motion, while public infrastructure remains deprioritized, Liminal imagines how bodies adapt to shifting environments when development is redirected. Voiced by conversations about land taken without notice, displacement, and the quiet erosion of what people depend on, the film draws on interviews with women living in a 1960s social housing development in Kaneshie to capture the conditions and somatic responses of communities inhabiting these incomplete structures, merging movement, sound, and architecture in a field of tension. - Nana Yaa Poku Asare-Boadu
items.title: ​Dancing About Architecture: Liminal

items.text: Lost in Air Writer-director Jessie Andrews explores longing, identity, sexuality, and the human desire to escape your own inner world for the poetic vignette Lost in Air . Set against the restless energy of Hong Kong, a withdrawn young man, Teo, drifts through a life that feels increasingly suffocating, marking his birthday chasing brief helium-induced highs. When he crosses paths with Meyling, a free-spirited American girl celebrating her own birthday, their parallel nights intersect in a fleeting moment of connection that awakens something deep within him, until she disappears back into the city. - Jessie Andrews When Teo is left suspended between illusion and reality, Lost in Air poses questions about temporary escapism and avoidance, and at what point he must confront the life he’s been ignoring. Leaning into surreal, dreamlike imagery, and fetishistic fantasy, Andrews frames the quietly transformative power of this brief encounter, in which fascination bridges desire, admiration, and the longing for a version of freedom that feels just out of reach.
items.title: Lost in Air

items.text: ​Scenes: Passinho A dance created in the 2000s by young people in Rio de Janeiro’s favelas, Passinho has been declared an “intangible cultural heritage” of the state of Rio – bringing recognition to a form of movement and expression born in the city's peripheral communities. For the short film Passinho , directors Jonangelo Molinari, Luiza Herdy, and Matheus Dafi connect with the group Passinho no Metrô, most of whom grew up in the Complexo de Alemão – which gained attention after a violent military operation targeted the neighborhood in 2025. - Matheus Dafi Making a living by dancing on the subway, Passinho no Metrô – which later became Palco do Passinho – uses public performance to dispel negative stereotypes of Brazilian favelas, and celebrate their unique culture through movement. Filmed in 2023, Passinho encounters the dancers between different dimensions of their daily lives – from Complexo do Alemão, to transforming the subway system into a stage – allowing art to open new possibilities, as a way of moving through the city and a particular period of their lives.

items.text: ​Private View: Betye Saar A lifelong collector who assembled found objects into poetic constellations of meaning, American artist Betye Saar emerged as a prominent force in the Black Arts Movement of the 1960s and ‘70s, creating powerful works that questioned their own cultural, political, and historical context. Born in Los Angeles in 1926 and raised in Pasadena, until her recent passing at 99, the California artist used her six-decade-spanning practice to reflect on African American identity, addressing themes of racial oppression, mysticism, the occult, family, and memory, while reframing symbols of Jim Crow-era America as radical statements of Black liberation. - Kyle Provencio Reingold In an excerpt from the short documentary Betye Saar: Drifting Toward Twilight , produced by The Huntington, director Kyle Provencio Reingold moves beyond the public mythology of the artist to reveal the quieter spaces between her remarkable career and personal realm, in moments of reflection on her life as an artist, mother, grandmother, and gatherer of objects. Connecting recent works with archival reflections, the film seeks to experience the world as Betye did, where history resides in everyday objects, spirituality emerges through careful observation, and storytelling becomes an act of preservation. Let's Get It On: The Wearable Art of Betye Saar is on view at Roberts Projects in Los Angeles until 22 August 2026. The full-length documentary Betye Saar: Drifting Toward Twilight is on view at The Huntington until 30 November 2027.
items.title: ​Private View: Betye Saar

items.text: ​Portrait of a Place: Un Canto por el Desierto Connecting with the Comcaac people on the Sonoran coastline in Mexico, director Enrique M. Rizo meets an Indigenous community held together by its women for the short film Un Canto por el Desierto – translated as A Song for the Desert . Numbering fewer than a thousand and among the last to maintain a truly nomadic desert-and-sea way of life, the Comcaac – also known as Seris – continue an ancestral basket weaving tradition, constructing woven vessels from the elephant plant, or torote, that support numerous daily needs, as carriers for food, grain, water, and babies. - Enrique M. Rizo Engaging with a local woman, Ana María, speaking in the Comcaac native language Cmiique Iitom, Un Canto por el Desierto moves beyond the simple logic of basket weaving, accessing ancestral knowledge though the paranormal and folkloric beliefs woven into the artform itself. Guided by an oral tradition embedded in the elements, with songs addressing the desert, the wind, the ocean, and the sun, Rizo documents a community with a profound connection to the unique geography of the landscape, the natural elements, and supernatural forces that defy explanation.
items.title: ​Portrait of a Place: Un Canto por el Desierto

items.text: ​NOWNESS Shorts: Turning 13 For the short film Turning 13 , director Stella Blackmon captures youth in the Ozarks, and days where it feels like nothing and everything is happening to you, reflecting on the emotions that mark the shift into teenagedom. Shooting in her hometown in Missouri during the hottest days of an Ozarks summer, Blackmon filmed family, friends and neighbors in her favorite childhood homes and alleyways, following her cousin Margot as she contemplates what it means to grow up in the two days before her 13th birthday. - Stella Blackmon Observing her cousins running lemonade stands to get money for pedicures and budget store makeup, Blackmon frames the early stages of adolescence against glimpses of their younger selves – putting dish soap in the stocktank pool, and curling up in their mom’s lap after a day at the river. Merging her own experience of 13 as having a foot in two different worlds with narration including real lines from Margot’s diary – like hiding her “stufted” animals before friends came over – Turning 13 distils the essence of ordinary moments specific to the Ozarks, building a world around vivid memories retold through a cinematic lens.

items.text: ​Video Art Visions: Romain Gavras & Surkin - Baikonur Imagining futures glimpsed from the margins, shaped less by collapse than by distortion, French filmmaker Romain Gavras and musician-producer Surkin build a multimedia world around peripheral dystopias for GENER8ION: Visions of 2034 – a major exhibition at London’s 180 Studios . The first of ten audiovisual works, observing familiar yet skewed environments, their experimental film Baikonur documents the world’s oldest space launch facility, the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan – a shadow of the Soviet era that remains under Russian control. Reflecting on how culture is consumed, processed, and forgotten, the video piece sits within a wider concept examining mutations between the reflexes of pleasure and the machinery of control – in response to cultural theorist Jean Baudrillard’s concept of simulation. Meditating on the spaceport’s unchanged infrastructure, and the moment a rocket launches into space, Gavras and Surkin consider the philosophy of freedom from a site that occupies a strange space in history – existing as a vision of what survives, and what doesn’t in an uncertain future. What first brought you to Kazakhstan? Romain Gavras: It’s the second time I went. I love the "Stans" – the layers of history, ancient and recent, in that part of the world are worn on the sleeves How did you land on the idea for the film? I was originally scouting for a secret project. We went with my line producer Guillaume Le François and my DOP André Chemetoff and when we got there we couldn’t stop shooting. What drew your attention to the Baikonur Cosmodrome? I’ve always been fascinated by it. It’s a Russian built enclave in the middle of the Kazakh desert, only made to support the Cosmodrome – like an ex-Soviet Truman Show for space exploration. At the time, it was the only place on Earth where they launched humans into space, so even our astronauts had to use the Russian infrastructures of Roscosmos to get up to space. It was also the only place in the world where you were allowed to film a rocket launched from only a kilometer away – Cape Canaveral, for example, is 8km. How did you go about creating a sense of dystopia? I didn’t really have to, it’s there. Built in the ‘50s , nothing has really moved, there is an amazing sense of purpose in the architecture of it, a sense that the future was going to be glorious – then time froze everything in that period. When I shot it, the only humans going to space were launched from there and every technological aspect is from the ‘70s – the bus the astronauts arrive at the rocket in, the train the rocket travels in. It’s fascinating. How did you guide the visual approach? It was really meant to be documentation for my own research, so it is very removed from a strong intention, very matter of fact and photo-like. How has your creative relationship with Surkin evolved? We’ve known each other since forever, and always liked to work together and talk about ideas about music and images. Can you talk us through some of the film’s themes, and how this relates to the exhibition as a whole? We open the exhibition with it. I feel it gives context about how history moves and the sentiment of the exhibit as a whole, which is constructed as a retrospective about a time in the future. Within this body of work, what message did you want the film to communicate? I’m not keen on straightforward messages, but I like the idea of creating a feeling, and the feelings I have about the future are dual. One take is that no matter what happens, there is still going to be poetry and beauty in the world, and kids will be kids doing silly things no matter the environment. My other take is that we all know that we’re dancing on the edge of a volcano. GENER8ION: Visions of 2034 will be on view at 180 Studios in London until 30 August 2026.
items.title: ​Video Art Visions: Romain Gavras & Surkin - Baikonur

items.text: Dancing About Architecture: On Time For the short film On Time , artist duos studiosyn_ (Fabian Blaschke and Lia von Buddenbrock) and Gerard & Kelly co-direct a cinematic response to the modernist architecture of Villa Benkemoun in Arles, France, reinterpreting their live performance ‘Clockwork’ – curated by Raphaël Giannesini, and presented during Les Rencontres d’Arles 2026. Created in dialogue with French architect Émile Sala’s 1974-designed residence, the evocative movement piece reflects on the passage of time and fleeting moments of everyday life, restoring the intimacy of domestic space to an architectural icon marked by its asymmetry and organic curving form. - Gerard & Kelly Developed by Bureau Future for Villa Benkemoun, On Time brings together two distinct creative practices to reinhabit Villa Benkemoun through movement and memory, shaping a poetic, contemplative journey through the villa’s rooms, halls, and striking exterior spaces. Appearing together and apart, falling in and out of sync, performers Georges Labbat and Matteo Manzoni are redoubled as shadows and reflections – while their ambiguous relationship is never fully explained – sensitively mirroring the architecture and its singular identity.
items.title: Dancing About Architecture: On Time

items.text: In On Rape and Institutional Failure, an exhibition centered on the second chapter of her ongoing project A History of Misogyny, Laia Abril examines different forms of violence against women throughout history.Weaving together images, compiled testimonies, archival materials, select objects, and installations with sound and video, the exhibition investigates how gender-based stereotypes, coupled with worldwide prejudices and misconceptions, have contributed to a systemic rape culture that persists today. By focusing on institutions, Abril aims to avoid narratives of victim-blaming, instead addressing the on-going problem of social accountability that has allowed offenders and enablers alike to avoid justice. On Rape and Institutional Failure was first exhibited in 2020 in the wake of the initial, galvanizing allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other powerful men. While #MeToo has led to few sustained consequences and little systemic change, Abril offers a meaningful opportunity to address the long history of silencing victims and the transgenerational trauma that has developed as a result. About Laia Abril:Laia Abril (b. 1986) is a research-based artist working across photography, text, video, and sound, focusing on biopolitics and gender issues. Her work is rooted in a politically engaged, process-driven methodology that employs strategies of forensic aesthetics and counter-narratives, interrogating dominant histories and the politics of representation.Her work has been exhibited in over 25 countries and is held in collections such as Centre Pompidou, Photo Elysée, Fotomuseum Winterthur, MACBA, Reina Sofía, MNAC, and the V&A Museum. She has authored acclaimed books, including The Epilogue, Lobismuller, and the A History of Misogyny series: On Abortion, On Rape, and On Mass Hysteria.She has received the Foam Paul Huf Award (Amsterdam), RPS Hood Medal (London), Aperture Best Book Award (NY/Paris), and Spain’s National Photography Award. Based in Switzerland, she is CONFIDENTIAL Last Updated: June 29, 2026 About Curator:Sara Ickow is the Associate Director of Exhibitions at the International Center of Photography, where she has been a curator on exhibitions including Gillian Laub: Family Matters, ICP at 50: From the Collection 1845–2019, To Conjure: New Archives in Recent Photography, and Photobooks USA 2000–25. She is also the Managing Director for Women Photograph and co-editor of the book Women Photograph: What We See. Previously, she worked as Curatorial Assistant and Collections Manager at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery. Sara holds an MA in Art History from NYU’s Institute of Fine Arts. items.text: In the 1960s, 70s, and 80s, movie theaters displayed photographs in their lobbies, offering audiences a glimpse of what awaited them beyond the box office. By contract, these materials were meant to be destroyed once a film’s run had ended. One of the most common ways to do so was to burn them in a vacant lot nearby. A cinephile projectionist in Colombia decided to keep them instead, and decades later an archive of nearly 10,000 of these images resurfaced in Medellín.Fuego Camina Conmigo is an edition of 300 numbered books, each one unique, made from that archive. Its pages are composed of original silver gelatin lobby cards and, on the reverse, risograph-printed frames from films in which fire appears. As the pages are turned, both images coexist for a brief moment and, for a fraction of a second, these photographs catch fire only in our eyes.The book also includes a short reflection by the publishers on the relationship between cinema and fire. Rather than producing an English-language version of the book, the publishers translated the text into a matchbook that accompanies the Spanish edition and includes a small cutout from one of the original lobby cards.For ICP’s Book on the Wall series, La Bruja Ediciones and Ediciones Réplica expanded the publication into an installation composed of the same materials found in the book: original movie posters, photographs, and risograph prints, accompanied by a projection of excerpts from fire scenes in the films. The installation takes the form of a modular wheat-pasted mural attached to one of the bookstore’s walls, bringing into focus the circulation, persistence, and afterlife of images. About the publishers Ediciones Réplica is an independent Colombian publishing collective and imprint founded by researchers and artists Arturo Salazar and José Ruiz. Its work focuses on the research, editing, and publication of photographic archives and printed culture from Latin America.Through photobooks, exhibitions, and curatorial projects, Ediciones Réplica gives new form to historical visual collections, bringing together archival research, popular graphic culture, and the material histories of photography.La Bruja Ediciones is an independent publishing studio and print workshop based in Medellín, Colombia, specializing in risograph printing. Run by Ximena Escobar and Andrew Smith they focused on artists’ books, zines, and small-run editions, the project combines manual printing techniques with carefully selected papers to produce numbered publications and graphic works rooted in material experimentation. About Book on the WallBooks are central to photography, as they are to our exhibitions, school and library here at ICP. Editing, sequencing, design and choice of materials are vital elements in the making of any photobook. For The Book on the Wall we invite publishers to give an insight into the making of a recent book through a one-wall feature in ICP's shop, which is free and open to the public seven days a week. SPANISHEn las décadas de 1960, 70 y 80, los cines mostraban fotografías en sus vestíbulos, ofreciendo al público un adelanto de lo que les esperaba al otro lado de la taquilla. Por contrato, estos materiales debían destruirse una vez finalizada la exhibición de la película. Una de las formas más habituales era quemarlos en algún lote baldío cercano. Un proyeccionista cinéfilo en Colombia decidió conservarlos y, décadas más tarde, un archivo de cerca de 10.000 de estas imágenes reapareció en Medellín.Fuego Camina Conmigo es una edición de 300 libros numerados, todos distintos entre sí, realizada a partir de ese archivo. Sus páginas están compuestas por fotografias originales impresas en gelatina de plata y, en el reverso, por fotogramas impresos en risografía de películas en las que aparece el fuego. Al pasar las páginas, ambas imágenes conviven por un instante y, durante una fracción de segundo, estas fotografías arden únicamente en nuestros ojos.El libro también incluye una breve reflexión de los editores sobre la relación entre cine y fuego. La traducción al inglés se presenta en forma de una caja de fósforos que acompaña la edición en español e incluye un pequeño recorte de una de las fotografias originales.Para la serie Book on the Wall del ICP, La Bruja Ediciones y Ediciones Réplica llevaron la publicación al espacio expositivo mediante una instalación. Un mural modular fijado con engrudo a una de las paredes de la librería, compuesto por los mismos materiales presentes en el libro, afiches originales de cine, fotografías e impresiones en risografía, se complementa con una proyección de fragmentos de escenas de fuego de las películas. En conjunto, la instalación dirige la mirada hacia la circulación y persistencia de las imágenes. Sobre los editoresEdiciones Réplica es un colectivo y sello editorial independiente colombiano fundado por los investigadores y artistas Arturo Salazar y José Ruiz. Su trabajo se centra en la investigación, edición y publicación de archivos fotográficos y cultura impresa de América Latina.A través de fotolibros, exposiciones y proyectos curatoriales, Ediciones Réplica da nuevas formas a colecciones visuales históricas y explora las relaciones entre los archivos, la gráfica popular y las historias materiales de la fotografía.La Bruja Ediciones es un taller y estudio de edición independiente con sede en Medellín, Colombia, especializado en impresión risográfica. Dirigido por Ximena Escobar y Andrew Smith, el proyecto produce libros de artista, fanzines y ediciones de pequeña escala, combinando técnicas de impresión manual con una cuidadosa selección de papeles para dar forma a publicaciones numeradas y obras gráficas marcadas por la experimentación material. Acerca de Book on the WallLos libros ocupan un lugar central en la fotografía, al igual que en nuestras exposiciones, nuestra escuela y nuestra biblioteca en ICP. La edición, la secuenciación, el diseño y la elección de los materiales son elementos fundamentales en la creación de cualquier fotolibro.Book on the Wall, ofrece a las editoriales la oportunidad de presentar el proceso creativo detrás de una publicación reciente a través de una instalación especial en una de las paredes de la tienda de ICP, un espacio gratuito y abierto al público los siete días de la semana.

items.text: ICP’s Incubator is located on ICP’s ground floor. The space is free and open to the public during café and museum hours. Photographer and ICP alum Andrea Hernández Briceño has been documenting the indigenous Huöttöja people in the Amazon basin since 2024. Many members of the Huöttöja community feel the pull of the mining industry, which promises to make them rich but threatens to dilute their culture. Hernández Briceño was invited to document their traditions and ancestral knowledge as a way to preserve them, but also set herself the goal to avoid being another outsider that left them feeling exploited. She aims to create a body of work that reflects the Huöttöja worldview and spirituality by nurturing a long term relationship with the community and its main goal: to show us that humans are not separate from nature, but an extension of it. About The ArtistAndrea Hernández Briceño is a Venezuelan journalist, visual storyteller, Magnum Foundation fellow, TEDx speaker and National Geographic explorer based in Caracas. She tells representative stories about gender, environment and social phenomena that put the dignity of participants in the center of the narrative while using different formats and a perceptive approach to magic. She was awarded the Women Photograph grant in 2024, three POY Latams (2023 and 2025) and has been shortlisted for the Marilyn Stafford Award twice. Hernández Briceño co-founded the all women collectives Ayün Fotógrafas and Solunar. She teaches the Ojo Pelao and MiraVzla free workshops, making photography education more accessible in her country. She believes in the importance of creating alliances with communities through horizontal practices that combine education, community building and storytelling initiatives. Her work explores narratives that search for humanity in the space between seemingly opposing ideas as a result of growing up, documenting and resisting in Venezuela, a place of deep contradictions. As part of a team effort she published a book called Mango Season that looks into food insecurity and the resolve to live a dignified life in Venezuela with Raya Editorial and El Archivo. Hernández Briceño collaborates with The Washington Post, The Guardian, El País and other international outlets. Her work has been exhibited in New York, Paris, Mexico City and Venezuela. About the ICP Incubator SpaceICP’s Incubator Space is a new exhibition program designed to highlight the work of emerging photographers who are responding in real time to the world around us. ICP will present a rotating selection of projects by imagemakers experimenting with and pushing boundaries around the documentary tradition. ICP’s Incubator Space is curated by Sara Ickow, Associate Director of Exhibitions at ICP. Header image: A light shines upon the tip of the Huöttöja communal home “churuata” in the Amazonas state, Venezuela, on April 21, 2025. In the indigenous Huöttöja people’s worldview, this branch functions as an antenna connecting the earth with the spiritual realm. The “churuata” is the place where shaman Jattupa tells the stories that conform the Huöttöja way of life, viewing humans not as separate from nature but as an extension of it.

items.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reconsiders and expands on the history of Japanese photography through the work twenty-eight intergenerational artists from the 1950s to today. Presented in partnership with Aperture and curated by Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko, the exhibition includes work Fujioka Aya, Hara Mikiko, Hiromix, Ishikawa Mao, Ishiuchi Miyako, Katayama Mari, Kawauchi Rinko, Komatsu Hiroko, Kon Michiko, Nagashima Yurie, Narahashi Asako, Ninagawa Mika, Nishimura Tamiko, Noguchi Rika, Nomura Sakiko, Okabe Momo, Okanoue Toshiko, Onodera Yuki, Sawada Tomoko, Shiga Lieko, Sugiura Kunié, Suzuki Nozomi, Tawada Yuki, Tokiwa Toyoko, Ushioda Tokuko, Watanabe Hitomi, Yamazawa Eiko and Yanagi Miwa.Spanning photography, installation, photobooks, and printed matter, the exhibition explores the experiences and perspectives of women in Japan through delicate and blunt observations of everyday life, critical reflections on the roles inhabited and reshaped by Japanese women, and approaches that push the boundaries of photography. The exhibition is accompanied by a major publication (Aperture, 2024) that expands upon content of the show through essays, historical material, and a comprehensive bibliography of photobooks made by Japanese women. About Curators:Lesley A. Martin is executive director of Printed Matter. Most recently, she was the creative director of Aperture, where she served as editor on more than one hundred books on photography, and as founding publisher of The PhotoBook Review. Takeuchi Mariko is a photography critic, curator, and professor at Kyoto University of the Arts. Previously, she served as visiting researcher at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, and at the National Museum of Art, Osaka. items.text: Yves Saint Laurent and Photography explores the powerful relationship Yves Saint Laurent forged between fashion and photography over four decades, revealing how photography functioned not only as a tool for promotion but also as a creative force that helped define a legacy. Organized in collaboration with the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris and the Fondation Pierre Bergé–Yves Saint Laurent, it brings together nearly 300 iconic photographs and archival objects.Featuring work by celebrated artists such as Richard Avedon, Cecil Beaton, Guy Bourdin, Robert Doisneau, Horst P. Horst, William Klein, Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, Duane Michals, Helmut Newton, Irving Penn, David Seidner, Andy Warhol, and others, the exhibition pairs these photographs with contact sheets, campaign materials, magazines, and personal images. Together, they reveal how Yves Saint Laurent established a blueprint for the way the fashion world is visualized and understood today.Curated by Simon Baker, Guest Curator and photography historian; Nastasia Alberti, Deputy Head of Collections and Head Archivist; and Clémentine Cuinet, Head of Photographic Collections, both of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris."The show takes visitors into the expansive visual universe of a designer whose work continues to shape how fashion is perceived today."– W Magazine "The show left me fascinated. Craving for more." - Musée Magazine"To see his clothes through the eyes of photographers such as Helmut Newton, Richard Avedon, David Bailey and more, as you do in the ICP show, is to see the way fashion and photography came together to crystallize moments of change in gender relations, culture, and society in the second half of the 20th century."—The New York Times About Yves Saint LaurentYves Mathieu-Saint-Laurent (b. 1936, Oran, Algeria) began his career in Paris in 1955 as an assistant to renowned couturier Christian Dior. Following Dior’s sudden death in 1957, Yves Saint Laurent was appointed artistic director of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris and his designs quickly gained critical acclaim. Dismissed from Dior in 1960 after military service and a subsequent hospitalization for depression, he founded his own couture house in partnership with Pierre Bergé, whom he had met in 1958. The first collection was presented in 1962 and the house became known for reinterpreting traditionally masculine garments like pantsuits and trench coats into bold, feminine looks that redefined the wardrobe of the modern woman. In 1966, he launched SAINT LAURENT rive gauche, a ready-to-wear line with stores opened internationally. Influenced by different cultures, Yves Saint Laurent’s designs paid tribute to artists including Mondrian, Picasso and Van Gogh and drew inspiration from faraway places––most notably Marrakech. This prolific output spanned thirty years and was the subject of numerous awards and exhibitions across the globe. Yves Saint Laurent retired and closed the couture house in 2002, at which point the newly-formed Fondation Pierre Bergé–Yves Saint Laurent assumed responsibility for advancing and safeguarding his work. Yves Saint Laurent died at his Paris home on June 1, 2008, at the age of seventy-one.In 2017, the Fondation Pierre Bergé–Yves Saint Laurent was re-envisioned with the opening of two museums in Paris and Marrakech. These institutions preserve and celebrate one of the twentieth century’s most defining creative legacies.About Musée Yves Saint Laurent ParisThe Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris, chaired by Madison Cox, is the first museum dedicated to one of the greatest couturiers of the twentieth century to open in the capital of fashion. It opened its doors on October 3, 2017, fifteen years after the closing of the haute couture house and obtained the designation ‘Musée de France.’ It occupies the historic hôtel particulier at 5 Avenue Marceau where for nearly thirty years, from 1974 to 2002, Yves Saint Laurent’s creative genius held sway. The museum's vast collection includes 12,000 garments, including 8,300 haute couture pieces more than 100,000 graphic artworks, including 55,000 fashion sketches by the couturier and 194,000 photographs comprising of diapositives, negatives and vintage and modern prints, as well as an archive of more than 4,000 magazines and 60,000 documents, including correspondence, audiovisual materials and personal objects, completing the collection. This ensemble is the result of the pioneering and systematic archival work initiated by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé. The Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris is temporarily closed for renovations. It is scheduled to reopen in the fall of 2027. Header image: Ensemble worn by Edia Vairelli, Haute Couture Spring/Summer 1982 collection, 5 Avenue Marceau, Paris, January 1982. items.text: AI needs no introduction. It’s wildly powerful. It ramped quickly and flooded every corner of our lives, and yes, a few big tech companies behaved like hooligans along the way, which naturally created fear, dread, and the sense that something precious was slipping away. But here’s the hard truth: AI has already been adopted. Every single photographer we’ve spoken to in the past six months, and that’s hundreds of them, is using it. Not as a philosophical debate. Not as an existential threat. Just as a tool to run their business. To build mood boards. To finish images. To keep up. AI is reshaping photography at a pace we haven’t seen since the transition from film to digital. And this is uncomfortable. Profoundly uncomfortable. But if there’s anything we’ve learned from Patrick Fore, we need to “sit with the discomfort.” So now the real question is: What future are we building toward? items.text: We followed art director Olivia Cho Lund as she captured her latest project, Finding You to Find Myself, a striking blend of surreal portraiture and deeply personal storytelling. We got the chance to see her own layered identity, and the collaborative energy of her team helped shape the project. Born and raised in Brazil, living in France, and now based in Denmark, Olivia has always carried a complex sense of self. But it was her Korean heritage, the “deepest hidden layer,” as she calls it, that inspired this journey. Along the way, she connected with Danish individuals who were subjected to adoption from Korea, people who, like her, navigate the intertwined paths of belonging and self-definition. “This project is an exploration of cultural identity, a red thread that weaves together immigrants, multicultural individuals, and those subjected to adoption, revealing one of the many facets that shape who we are: our Koreanness.” From makeup dusted with gochugaru, to gestures frozen mid-movement, to surreal camera effects revealing inner worlds, every detail was intentional. items.text: Francis Tama, visual creator and founder of post-production studio Casa Dusk, has a strong editorial eye and is the creative mind behind many fashion, beauty, and still-life photoshoots. In spring, Francis took on the creative direction of Starlight, a fashion editorial for PAP Magazine. Featuring delicate contrasts between light and shadow, rich textures, and emotive color palettes, the editorial was built with intention: clean, calm, and focused. What makes Starlight unique, is that it was created entirely remotely. Francis decided to collaborate with people he’d met while living abroad, after he’d connected deeply with them both personally and creatively. Starlight, conceptualized by Tama and Casa Dusk studio, was the result of a harmonious collaboration, a shared visual language and trust.
